knowledge_point.title: Evaluating a Double Integral by Converting To Polar Coordinates

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate 

$$
\iint_D 3 e^{x^{2} + y^{2}}\,dA
$$

, where $D$ is the disk $x^2+y^2\le 4$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ and $dA=r\,dr\,d\theta$, with $r\ge0$.

The Cartesian restrictions give the following polar region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-28-topic-audit-3/published-probe/17592186129200/region-74de6b02dbcb67247ed0.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}0\le r&\le 2 \\
0\le\theta&\le 2 \pi\end{aligned}
$$
Here $x^2+y^2=r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=r^2$.
For the radial primitive, set $u=r^2$, so $du=2r\,dr$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 3 e^{x^{2} + y^{2}}\,dA&=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_0^{2}3 r e^{r^{2}}\,dr\,d\theta \\
&=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left[\frac{3 e^{r^{2}}}{2}\right]_0^{2}\,d\theta \\
&=\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\left(- \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3 e^{4}}{2}\right)\,d\theta \\
&=\left[\frac{\theta \left(-3 + 3 e^{4}\right)}{2}\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\
&=\left(\pi \left(-3 + 3 e^{4}\right)\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=3 \pi \left(-1 + e^{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$
